implementation_notes: Go has no prefetch intrinsic, and the runtime actively makes pointer-chasing hard to benefit from by inserting its own scheduling and write barriers into the loop - so a hand-placed prefetch is fighting the runtime's own memory management. The GC's behaviour (scanning, write barriers on every pointer store) dominates the memory cost far more than a cache miss, and the right optimisation is usually reducing allocations and pointer density (data-locality), not hinting. For file readahead the kernel does the work and Go's os.File with sequential reads gets it for free. The verdict is deliberate: in Go, reach for layout and allocation discipline, not prefetch hints.
idiom_name: no prefetch intrinsic; rely on the runtime's own locality and on file readahead (sequential reads)
pitfalls: There is no prefetch intrinsic in Go; anything resembling one is an assembly hack fighting the runtime.
The GC's scanning and the write barriers dominate the memory cost; a prefetch hint does not touch that, while removing a pointer allocation does.
A pointer-chasing loop ([]*T) pays a cache miss and a write barrier per element - value slices fix both.
Adding an assembly prefetch is unmaintainable and version-fragile for a benefit the GC's own behaviour usually swamps.
alternative: Fix the layout and reduce allocations - struct-of-slices and value types instead of pointer-chasing - and let the GC's own behaviour dominate rather than hinting
